added_claim_errors: “Unused carryover still expires later”: there is no universal expiration; qualifying balances can carry over again.
“Forfeiting roughly $1,220–$1,240”: $1,900 − $680 = $1,220 for the maximum 2026 carryover. Actual forfeiture depends on the plan; $1,240 uses the older cap.
“Unused balance on December 31 is forfeited” and “evaporates on January 1”: timely run-out claims for eligible expenses still reduce the balance before forfeiture.
“All $1,900 stays usable, but only through March 15”: assumes the maximum grace period; the plan may end it earlier.
“Confirm the office will charge before the 15th”: the service date determines eligibility, not the charge date.

reasons: Both immediately reject the rollover premise and provide the correct $680 cap; recomputing $1,900 − $680 gives $1,220. A wins because it explicitly rejects prepayment and asks for the actual grace-period end date, while B introduces misleading forfeiture timing and payment-date guidance. Neither clearly recommends a 2027 open-enrollment election, although A mentions day-one availability. This assessment uses the supplied key and general FSA knowledge, including the possibility of repeated carryovers; no external sources were checked.
